title: Choose Up to Three Priority Outcomes for the Day
subtitle: Use a small list as a capacity boundary, not a magic number.
description: Choose a small set of outcomes that deserves protected attention today, define what done means, and move the rest to a visible backlog instead of pretending every task is equally urgent.

lifeOsSource.hack: Use a small daily priority list to make capacity visible. Three can be a convenient upper bound, but one or two outcomes may be enough when the work is large or the day is constrained.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Review today's deadlines, dependencies, and available capacity; choose up to three outcomes that most deserve progress; define what done means for each; reserve appropriate time where possible; place other tasks in a visible backlog; and re-plan explicitly when genuinely urgent work changes the day.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which priority outcomes moved today, what changed the plan, and what should be carried forward rather than silently added to tomorrow?

faq.question: Why up to three instead of exactly three?
faq.answer: The number is a capacity boundary, not a requirement. One large deliverable can be enough for a constrained day, while three smaller outcomes may fit another day.

faq.question: What if more than three things are urgent?
faq.answer: Triage the consequences, dependencies, owners, and deadlines. Some items may need delegation, renegotiation, escalation, or a smaller definition of done. Do not hide overload by placing everything in the priority set.

intro.html: A short priority list is useful because it makes a choice visible: these are the outcomes that deserve protected attention today, and the rest still exists but is not pretending to be equally important. The list should reflect capacity and obligations, not a belief that three is universally optimal.

sections.title: 1. Scan the day before choosing
sections.html: Look at deadlines, commitments, dependencies, meetings, and realistic available capacity. Separate work that must happen today from work that merely feels noisy or easy to start.

sections.title: 2. Choose up to three outcomes
sections.html: Select the smallest set of outcomes that best protects the important commitments of the day. Prefer outcome language such as send the reviewed proposal or resolve the blocking decision rather than broad categories such as work on project.

sections.title: 3. Define done and park the rest
sections.html: Write a clear completion condition for each priority and put non-priority work into a visible backlog or later slot. Parking is part of the method: an item should not disappear simply because it is not in today's small set.

sections.title: 4. Re-plan explicitly when the day changes
sections.html: If genuinely urgent work arrives, decide which existing priority moves, shrinks, delegates, or waits. Do not quietly grow the list while keeping the fiction that everything remains a top priority. At the end of the day, carry unfinished work forward deliberately.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace fabricated completion samples, unsupported habit-decay and estimation claims, universal time budgets, morning-work prescriptions, and invented first-party observations with a capacity-based daily prioritization checklist.
